key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months, but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, and actually increased missed payments among some nudged cardholders.
methodology: Field experiment on credit card autopay enrollment with 6-month follow-up; liquidity-constraint analysis explains heterogeneous response.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the core worry in the brief: a nudge can shift nominal enrollment/behavior without changing the underlying financial outcome, and can even create new harms (missed payments) for liquidity-constrained users — exactly the disengagement/complaint risk our support team flagged.
limitations: credit card minimum payments differ structurally from round-up savings
effect measured on payment behavior, not a save/enrollment default per se
relevance_reason: Consumer fintech field experiment showing a default-like nudge changes nominal behavior but not the underlying financial outcome, with real harms to liquidity-constrained users.

key_finding: Narrative synthesis of DC plan design finds automatic enrollment and default investment options raise short-term participation but carry longer-term engagement costs, with newer levers (auto-escalation, emergency savings accounts) proposed to offset this.
methodology: Narrative literature overview; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the current state-of-the-art summary of the employer-plan literature the brief says is the closest analogy — useful background, but its employer-plan setting caps its direct applicability to our consumer product decision.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer self-directed product
no effect sizes given in the abstract
narrative rather than systematic review
relevance_reason: Comprehensive recent overview of default effects in retirement plans, useful context though not our setting.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment in retirement plans functions as a 'passive trap': employees anchor at low contribution rates and disengage, so participation gains alone do not demonstrate welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative/opinion synthesis of existing empirical literature; abstract-only, no new data or effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Directly states the support team's counter-argument in explicit form — enrolment numbers can be vanity metrics if paired with disengagement — but its evidence base is retirement-plan literature, not a consumer product.
limitations: employer retirement setting, not consumer app
no primary data or quantified effect sizes
short opinion-style article with zero citations so far
relevance_reason: Articulates the exact 'passive trap' concern the brief raises, even though grounded in pension-plan evidence.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for when default effects persist, decay, or reverse downstream, identifying time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
methodology: Conceptual review and framework synthesis across the consumer-behavior default literature; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a general, non-employer-specific framework for exactly the question the brief asks — will enrolment persist or decay — and names the moderators (antecedent preference, salience of trade-offs) we should measure once we launch.
limitations: theoretical/synthesis paper, not new empirical data
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: General consumer-behavior review directly addressing whether and when defaults produce lasting versus decaying downstream effects.

key_finding: Using natural experiments and random assignment to default options, beneficiary passivity in Medicare Part D is large, persistent, and essentially insensitive to the value of the default, even when it causes substantial losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments with random assignment to default options in a government drug benefit program.
why_it_matters: Strong causal evidence that default persistence is not conditional on the default being a good one for the person — a distributional/manipulation-risk finding relevant to who gets hurt by an always-on default.
limitations: government health insurance program, not a consumer financial app
low-income Medicare population differs from our user base
relevance_reason: Rigorous natural-experiment evidence on how insensitive default adherence is to default quality, informing distributional risk even though the setting is health insurance.

key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, automatic enrollment raises steady-state saving rates by only 0.6% of income and default auto-escalation by only 0.3%, because only 40% of auto-escalation defaults are retained past the first escalation date.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, balance withdrawal, and auto-escalation opt-out.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: medium/long-run attrition and opt-out shrink the measured effect of both enrollment and level defaults far below the headline sign-up number.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated enrollment mechanism doesn't carry over to a self-directed app
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise with quantified medium/long-run attrition data, though in an employer-plan setting.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, but most affected individuals actively opted back out, with the default effect strongest among those unaware of their enrollment status.
methodology: Natural policy experiment using linked administrative and survey data on a nationwide auto-enrollment rollout.
why_it_matters: Quantifies a clean opt-out default effect size (23pp) and shows it is driven substantially by lack of awareness rather than genuine preference — a distributional/manipulation-risk signal for who is actually helped by defaulting people in.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension, not a consumer savings app
government-mandated rather than firm-chosen default
relevance_reason: Recent, well-identified default-enrollment effect size with evidence that awareness (not preference) drives adherence.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to participation and contributions, replicated at 12 months, attenuates substantially by 36 months, though it still reduces savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits this with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK representative panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly shows the enrolment-versus-persistence gap the brief worries about, with the added nuance that even attenuated defaults can meaningfully reduce inequality in outcomes — relevant to who benefits.
limitations: retirement savings context with long horizons, not liquid short-term savings
employer/plan administrator mediated enrollment
relevance_reason: Recent, well-powered evidence on medium-run attenuation of default effects and on distributional (inequality) impact.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person five-country European sample, defaults produce medium-to-large effects on risk-taking, but implementing a default (especially one participants refuse) lowers trust and rating of the advisor delivering it.
methodology: Three experiments, one a large representative multi-country European sample, testing default and framing manipulations on investment risk allocation.
why_it_matters: Gives EU-context experimental evidence that a default can backfire on trust/perceived honesty when refused — precisely the dark-pattern reputational risk the brief flags, and directly informs how to frame the multiplier default so it doesn't read as manipulative.
limitations: wealth-management advice context rather than round-up savings
no measurement of persistence beyond the experimental session
relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-advice experiments quantifying when a default is perceived as manipulative, directly bearing on reputational risk of opt-out design.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three firms, but roughly 80% of participants simply accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still doing so after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking 401(k) participation and default acceptance over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that people anchor on whatever default level is set — the single strongest piece of foundational evidence for the multiplier-anchoring risk in the level decision, even though newer studies have revised its magnitude down.
limitations: undated/older employer 401(k) study the field has since revised
retirement contribution rates, not a liquid round-up multiplier
relevance_reason: The foundational anchoring-on-default-level study that the newer literature (e.g. auto-escalation papers) argues with.

key_finding: A structural model on 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence comes from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost, and shows adding a lower preset option (15%) to an existing 20/25/30% menu captures 69% of achievable consumer welfare gain at 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million NYC taxi transactions, validated against a stated-preference survey; counterfactual menu-design simulation.
why_it_matters: The clearest available evidence on how a preset menu of options (directly analogous to a 1x/2x/5x multiplier menu) anchors choices and how adding/adjusting menu items trades off welfare against revenue — a direct methodological template for the level decision.
limitations: tipping decisions rather than savings
single transaction choice, not a persistent enrollment decision
relevance_reason: Consumer preset-menu decision study structurally identical in form to the multiplier-menu design question, quantifying anchoring and welfare trade-offs.

key_finding: An opt-in payroll short-term liquid savings account at five UK firms saw very low take-up (under 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated one), but among those who did enroll, 96% still held a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a payroll-deduction short-term savings program introduction at five UK firms with 12-month account-level tracking.
why_it_matters: Shows opt-in alone, even for a liquid, withdrawable product much like ours, produces very low enrolment but strong persistence among those who do enroll — useful evidence that the entry mechanism (not product design) is what needs fixing if opt-in is chosen.
limitations: employer payroll-based intermediary, unlike our direct-to-consumer app
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice conditions
relevance_reason: Closest available analog to round-up savings (liquid, withdrawable, small sums) showing opt-in take-up and persistence rates, despite the employer-payroll channel.

key_finding: Characterizes when weighted opt-out minimization (versus maximization) is the asymptotically optimal default design, extending to cases with externalities, fees, and designer-chooser disagreement about value.
methodology: Theoretical/asymptotic economic model with numerical simulations validating the approximations; abstract-only, no applied setting.
why_it_matters: Offers a general normative framework for choosing default policy under disagreement about the activity's value — relevant to deciding whether to default users into round-up saving when their true preference is uncertain — though it is not applied to any real setting.
limitations: purely theoretical with simulated validation, no empirical application
no named population or product setting
relevance_reason: General optimal-default-design theory that could inform the framework for choosing between opt-in/opt-out/active-choice, though untested empirically.

key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations used by EU law to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence (including pre-selected defaults) from regulable dark patterns.
methodology: Legal/normative analysis mapping EU dark-pattern law; abstract-only for empirical content.
why_it_matters: Gives the specific EU legal test for when an opt-out or pre-set multiplier crosses from 'helpful default' into 'dark pattern,' directly shaping how the entry and level decisions should be worded and disclosed to stay outside reputational/legal risk.
limitations: normative/legal analysis, not an empirical measurement of enrollment or saving effects
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the brief's named concern that an opt-out default could read as manipulative under EU consumer law.

key_finding: Under a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (vs ~50% opt-out under lower defaults), and those remaining at 12% earned notably lower incomes than predicted, showing the default anchored many onto a suboptimal contribution level.
methodology: Empirical analysis of employer retirement plan administrative data comparing a high (12%) default against a literature-reviewed baseline of lower defaults.
why_it_matters: Shows a high preset default strongly anchors contribution levels and disproportionately affects lower-income, less-engaged savers — a caution for pre-selecting a specific round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app the employer as trusted intermediary mechanism the brief says doesn't transfer
locked, illiquid savings unlike the round-up product
relevance_reason: Best available quantitative evidence on anchoring to a preset contribution level, though in the employer-plan setting the brief flags as only analogous.

key_finding: Abstract text is not available (truncated to a single word), so no substantive finding can be extracted.
methodology: abstract-only; title indicates four large UK field experiments on automating short-term payroll savings.
why_it_matters: Short-term, non-retirement payroll savings automation is a closer analogue to a liquid round-up product than pension research, but with no usable abstract content it cannot currently inform the decision.
limitations: abstract is essentially empty/corrupted
payroll-based savings still involves an employer channel, unlike a standalone consumer app
relevance_reason: Title suggests directly relevant short-term-savings automation evidence, but the abstract provides no extractable content.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts reduced unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide, though alerts captured less than half of consumers' potential savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments run by major UK retail banks on automatic enrollment into SMS alerts.
why_it_matters: This is the closest real-world precedent to the round-up feature: a UK consumer bank auto-enrolling customers into a financial behavior nudge with measured, sizeable benefit and no employer intermediary, giving a credible upper bound for what an opt-out design could achieve in this exact setting.
limitations: measures charge reduction, not savings-pot balances or long-run engagement/withdrawal behavior
alerts are a passive notification, not a recurring money-movement commitment like round-ups
relevance_reason: Directly on-point: UK consumer bank auto-enrollment experiment with quantified benefit and no employer-trust mechanism, matching the brief's setting closely.

key_finding: Over 41 months, automatic pension enrollment raised average savings by £32-38/month but was partially offset by a £7/month rise in unsecured debt and higher mortgage take-up, though loan defaults fell and credit scores rose modestly.
methodology: Natural experiment using the randomized UK roll-out of automatic enrollment pensions across ~160,000 small employers.
why_it_matters: Shows that a headline enrollment/savings gain from a default can be substantially offset by other financial behavior, supporting the support team's worry that a rising enrollment number may not translate into net financial benefit.
limitations: employer pension, not a consumer self-directed liquid savings product
debt-offset dynamics may not apply to small, voluntary round-up amounts
relevance_reason: Directly challenges the 'defaults straightforwardly help' premise by quantifying an offsetting cost of automatic enrollment, even though the setting is an employer pension.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' (an extra step) to a health-insurance auto-enrollment policy reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Policy evaluation of the removal of an auto-enrollment feature in health insurance, using a simple selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that even small frictions (analogous to opt-in vs opt-out) can produce large, distributionally uneven enrollment drops, informing how seriously to weigh the equity costs of choosing opt-in over opt-out for the round-up feature.
limitations: public health-insurance selection market, not a consumer savings product
no employer or app-based mediation, and no financial-product analogue for the selection dynamics
relevance_reason: Strong quantitative evidence on default/friction effects on enrollment and who is differentially excluded, though in a different (public insurance) market.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised campaign donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest effects on small, inexperienced donors who had not intended to commit to recurring payments.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting the different timing of prechecked-box rollouts across 2020 US campaign websites.
why_it_matters: The closest real-world precedent for a recurring-money default in a consumer, self-directed setting: it shows defaults can lift nominal sign-up while generating regret (refunds) concentrated among the least experienced users — exactly the disengagement/complaint risk the support team is warning about for round-ups.
limitations: political donations, not a banking/savings product
US setting, not EU consumer-protection regime
refunds are a proxy for regret, not a direct measure of withdrawal or 6-12 month persistence
relevance_reason: Provides a close consumer-facing analogue — a prechecked recurring financial commitment — with distributional evidence on who is harmed by the default, directly speaking to the brief's manipulation-risk question.

key_finding: In a search model and lab experiments, a default option raises the reservation utility (a reference effect) and also causes higher-value searchers to self-select into rejecting the default, both improving realized choice quality.
methodology: Theoretical search model with reference-dependent utility, tested in lab experiments; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a general mechanism (reference effects, self-selection) for why defaults can shape choice quality, but says nothing about financial enrollment, persistence, or amounts saved.
limitations: generic lab search task, no financial-product or app context
no enrollment, retention, or amount-saved outcomes measured
relevance_reason: Tangential general-economics evidence on default mechanisms with little direct bearing on the two named design decisions.

key_finding: Mandated EU active-choice browser screens produced large, persistent shifts in default-alternative usage — Firefox usage was 113% higher on iOS and 12% higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects still visible 15+ months later.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the staggered EU Digital Markets Act rollout of mandatory choice screens on iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: The most direct recent evidence that a forced active-choice screen, imposed under EU digital-market regulation, produces large and durable behavior change in a mobile-app context — directly informing whether active choice can substitute for opt-out on the entry decision.
limitations: browser default switching, not financial enrollment or savings amounts
platform-level aggregate data, no individual heterogeneity or engagement/withdrawal measures
relevance_reason: Closest available real-world test of active choice under EU regulation in a mobile app, giving persistence data code C6 and C2 need.

key_finding: In a 410-participant usability study, generalizable opt-out privacy schemes slightly reduced opt-out precision but substantially reduced disruption (98% not feeling disrupted for the least-disruptive scheme, a 40-point improvement over baseline), while 83% of participants understood the mechanism.
methodology: Design and usability study of nine privacy opt-out interface schemes implemented as a browser extension, tested with 410 participants.
why_it_matters: Shows a concrete design pattern for making a non-default, active-choice opt-out feel low-friction and non-disruptive — directly relevant to designing an active-choice onboarding screen for the round-up feature that doesn't feel punitive.
limitations: US privacy law (CCPA) context, not EU consumer/financial regulation
privacy consent setting, not a financial savings decision
relevance_reason: Offers a transferable interface-design lesson for making active/opt-out choice low-friction, relevant to the entry-decision UX even though the legal and product domain differ.

key_finding: Opt-out defaults increased sign-up (task uptake) in university exam registration, but for effortful outcomes requiring follow-through, the default only improved actual completion for individuals who were already responsive to university communication; non-responsive individuals showed increased sign-ups with no effect on real outcomes.
methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out for a single exam and for many exams.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the brief's central worry in a controlled setting: an opt-out default can inflate nominal enrollment while doing nothing for the behavior that actually matters, and the effect is concentrated in already-engaged users — exactly the heterogeneity question the round-up decision needs answered.
limitations: university exam registration, not a financial product or consumer app
no data on withdrawal, complaints, or amounts saved
relevance_reason: Cleanest available evidence that opt-out defaults can decouple nominal sign-up from real engagement, which is the exact mechanism the support team's objection describes, even though the setting is academic rather than financial.

key_finding: After target-date funds became allowable retirement-plan defaults, younger workers who started post-policy invested more in equities and older workers less, tracking the TDF glidepath, while contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel analysis of millions of US middle-class investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the Pension Protection Act's TDF default change.
why_it_matters: Shows a preset default can strongly anchor an allocation-type choice (glidepath) even while leaving contribution-rate behavior largely unaffected, a useful caution that a preset multiplier might shape one dimension of behavior but not another.
limitations: employer retirement plan investment allocation, not a consumer savings contribution decision
no data on enrollment or short-term liquid savings behavior
relevance_reason: Relevant evidence on default anchoring for a preset parameter, but in an employer-plan investment-allocation context rather than the brief's consumer setting.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension saving relative to a control group, with default-option and positive-narrative nudges producing the largest backfire effects, and with heterogeneity by income, education, gender, and financial motivation.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions in China.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the internal argument that 'defaults will lift enrollment' by showing default options can backfire and reduce willingness to contribute, reinforcing the need to test rather than assume a default's direction of effect for this specific product and population.
limitations: Chinese cultural/institutional context, not EU
hypothetical online survey rather than a live consumer product with real money
no persistence or amount-saved data beyond stated willingness
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the shortlist that a default option can reduce rather than raise engagement with saving, directly undermining the brief's stated 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people generally approved of financial nudges (rated neutral-to-positive) with strong preferences for System-2 (reflective) interventions and savings-framed messaging, regardless of transparency or whether a bank was the messenger.
methodology: Pre-registered survey experiment presenting 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios varying transparency, framing, and System-1/2 targeting to a representative Australian sample (n=2,100).
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether people perceive bank-driven financial nudges as manipulative or helpful, showing savings-framed, System-2 interventions are best-received — evidence for how to frame the round-up feature's entry screen to avoid a dark-pattern perception.
limitations: Hypothetical scenarios, not actual enrollment behavior
Does not measure enrollment or retention rates
Australian sample, not EU
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the manipulation/dark-pattern risk criterion for consumer financial nudges.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a choice between cash and bank-account transfer had no significant average effect on savings, but increased balances among those with nonpositive prior savings.
methodology: Field experiment with conditional cash transfer beneficiaries comparing cash vs. bank-account delivery of subsidies; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Shows that offering a savings vehicle mainly helps those with the least prior savings, a distributional pattern loosely relevant to who benefits from an enrollment default.
limitations: Developing-country conditional cash transfer population, not EU banking app users
Concerns payment-method choice, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice enrollment
No amount-saved effect sizes beyond balances
relevance_reason: Provides distributional evidence on savings behavior only weakly analogous to the round-up enrollment decision.

key_finding: The abstract (garbled/incomplete) suggests an automatic IRA program with an emergency-savings component preserves equal liquid-fund benefits regardless of contribution timing.
methodology: abstract-only; unclear design, likely a report on automatic IRA program outcomes.
why_it_matters: Touches on combining automatic enrollment with liquid emergency savings, relevant to the round-up feature's liquidity angle, but gives no usable effect sizes.
limitations: Abstract is fragmentary and largely uninformative
US automatic IRA context, not EU consumer app
No quantified enrollment or persistence data available
relevance_reason: Nominally on-topic (automatic enrollment + emergency/liquid savings) but too little information to use.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and most automatically-enrolled employees stuck to the default contribution rate and default fund allocation even years later.
methodology: Before/after administrative-data analysis of a single large US corporation's 401(k) plan following a switch from opt-in to automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: Establishes the foundational default-effect and anchoring findings the current literature (and this brief) argues with, setting the scale of enrollment lift and anchoring the project should benchmark against, while flagging the employer-as-advisor mechanism the brief says does not carry over.
limitations: Employer-sponsored 401(k), invoking the employer-trust mechanism the brief says doesn't apply
Single-firm case study
No manipulation/dark-pattern framing analysis
relevance_reason: The classic default-effect and anchoring study that current consumer-savings literature responds to.

key_finding: Abstract not available; the paper reportedly compares savings behaviors between automatic and voluntary enrollment in a defined-contribution retirement plan.
methodology: abstract-only; unknown design.
why_it_matters: Could add another automatic-vs-voluntary comparison point, but with no abstract there is nothing concrete to act on.
limitations: No abstract provided, so no usable findings
Retirement plan setting, not consumer fintech
relevance_reason: Topically on-point (auto vs voluntary enrollment) but unusable without abstract content.

key_finding: Institutional mistrust and minority status are each associated with both under-saving and early withdrawal from a previously-mandatory pension scheme in Estonia, a 'double jeopardy' pattern.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension-freedom reform introducing an early-withdrawal option.
why_it_matters: Warns that groups already saving too little are also most likely to withdraw early once given the option — relevant heterogeneity for who is helped or hurt by an easy-exit round-up feature.
limitations: Mandatory pension savings context, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
Correlational survey design, not causal identification of a default's effect
No enrollment-default effect size reported
relevance_reason: Distributional evidence on who under-saves and withdraws early, relevant to who is helped vs hurt by passive enrollment.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrollment vaccination policy reduced their stated intention to comply and reduced policy approval.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment across G7 countries testing reflection/transparency prompts about a hypothetical default-enrollment COVID-19 booster policy.
why_it_matters: Directly counters the assumption that defaults are costless: making the default salient can reduce approval and intent, a caution for how transparently the round-up feature's opt-out design should be surfaced to avoid backlash.
limitations: Public-health/vaccination setting, not financial
Hypothetical policy vignette, not actual enrollment behavior
No consumer financial context
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults straightforwardly help by showing reflection on a default can backfire, a caution for dark-pattern risk.

key_finding: Among US Millennials, automatic enrollment and employer matching contributions were both associated with higher likelihood of retirement plan participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study, controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance and assets.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the standard default-effect finding in a modern cohort but in an employer-plan setting, adding little new evidence about consumer self-directed enrollment.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plan, not consumer fintech
Cross-sectional/correlational, not a natural experiment
No persistence or withdrawal data beyond initial participation
relevance_reason: A modern replication of employer-plan default effects, useful only as background context.

key_finding: Using 41 million observations in Denmark, automatic employer contributions raised total retirement wealth substantially, while subsidies requiring active choice mostly shifted savings between accounts (each $1 of subsidy raised total saving by only 1 cent); ~85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but heavily moved by automatic contributions, and these passive savers are less wealthy and less financially sophisticated.
methodology: Population-level administrative panel data analysis for Denmark distinguishing active-saver and passive-saver responses to tax subsidies versus automatic employer contributions.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence that passive/default policies change actual saved amounts far more than active-choice policies, and that non-responders to active choice are the less-wealthy majority — a strong distributional argument for defaults, tempered by a retirement/tax-account setting rather than a liquid consumer product.
limitations: Danish retirement/taxable accounts with employer- and tax-mediated mechanisms, not a self-directed liquid consumer app
Automatic contributions are employer-administered, reintroducing the trusted-intermediary mechanism the brief says doesn't carry over
No manipulation/dark-pattern analysis
relevance_reason: Landmark large-N evidence that defaults move actual saved amounts, not just nominal participation, directly bearing on the brief's core amount-vs-enrollment question.

key_finding: Field experiments show that requiring an active choice (no default) increases engagement relative to no intervention, and an 'enhanced active choice' design that frames the non-preferred option as a loss further shifts behavior toward the favored alternative without an automatic-enrollment default.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and a modified 'enhanced active choice' (loss-framing the non-chosen option) against no-default and default conditions, drawing on savings and health behavior-change literature.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, transferable design technique for the app's active-choice onboarding screen — framing the decline option as a loss — that could capture much of opt-out's enrollment benefit without imposing a default, directly shaping the entry-mechanism decision.
limitations: Primary field experiments are in medication adherence, though savings applications are explicitly discussed
Does not report enrollment persistence at 6-12 months
Effect sizes not given in the abstract
relevance_reason: The core methods paper proposing and testing active choice / enhanced active choice as an alternative to automatic enrollment, whose loss-framing technique directly transfers to the app's onboarding screen design.

key_finding: This review synthesizes household-finance evidence on consumption/savings, borrowing, payments, and asset allocation, and surveys interventions — education, peer effects, product design, disclosure, and choice architecture — that shape household financial behavior.
methodology: Narrative review/book chapter synthesizing the behavioral household finance literature; not a systematic-review protocol.
why_it_matters: Serves as the broad synthesis anchor for the choice-architecture question, situating default and product-design effects within the wider consumer (not employer-plan) household finance literature the brief asks us to draw on.
limitations: Broad narrative overview rather than a quantitative meta-analysis with effect sizes
Covers many financial domains, not round-up savings specifically
Some included studies still draw heavily on employer-retirement literature
relevance_reason: The review/synthesis needed to check the shortlist against the wider behavioral household finance evidence base.

key_finding: At three large US firms, automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted (and half still followed after three years) the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, largely offsetting participation gains against under-saving from anchoring on the default rate.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large US firms comparing 401(k) participation, contribution rates, and asset allocation before/after automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a pre-set default level strongly anchors the amount people contribute — direct evidence for the anchoring risk when choosing which round-up multiplier (1x/2x/5x) to pre-select, warning that a low pre-selected multiplier could suppress contributions for years.
limitations: Employer-sponsored 401(k) plans, not a consumer liquid savings product
Default anchoring is on contribution rate/fund choice, not a round-up multiplier
Sample limited to three large US employers
relevance_reason: Foundational evidence that pre-set default levels anchor contribution choices for years, directly relevant to the level (C3) decision.

key_finding: Randomly assigning Afghan employees to default enrollment in a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points — equivalent to a 50% matching incentive — driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of choosing, and defaults also increased subsequent active/voluntary saving after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among Afghan government employees testing default enrollment variants in a salary-linked savings account, with follow-up interventions to identify mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Quantifies a large default effect (40pp) and shows some persistence into post-study active saving behavior, and identifies the psychological mechanism (present bias, choice-cost) that predicts whether a round-up default will keep working once users can freely exit.
limitations: Employer/government salary-linked savings account, not a self-directed banking app
Afghanistan context differs sharply from EU regulatory and liquidity environment
Persistence measured as post-study attitude/decision change, not 6-12 month withdrawal or amount-saved data
relevance_reason: Provides a quantified default effect size and mechanism evidence directly on point for the default-effect and persistence questions, despite a different employer/government setting.

key_finding: Payment reminders cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with the unintended harm concentrated in users with an overdraft history, who saw a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, testing payment reminder nudges on credit card and checking account behaviour.
why_it_matters: Direct, quantified evidence that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — exactly the distributional risk the brief flags for the round-up feature; argues for segmenting rollout and monitoring by user risk profile rather than assuming a uniform default helps everyone.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
Brazilian credit card/checking account context, not EU round-up savings
no data on persistence beyond the fee outcomes measured
relevance_reason: Provides concrete evidence of heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects of a nudge in a self-directed consumer financial product, directly informing the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk question (C5).
